asr.full_text: Let's kick off with why we are specifically in San Diego. You're just kicking off your annual bus tour. You go and visit branches and meet lots of your employees. What's the biggest thing you've learned from that process over the years? PATH, NOT SAN FRANCISCO AND L.A., BUT MALIBU, SAN DIEGO, ET CETERA. THESE ARE BOTH CLIENTS AND EMPLOYEES. WE LEARN A TREMENDOUS AMOUNT. WHAT WE CAN DO BETTER AS A COMPANY, WHAT FOLKS WOULD LIKE TO HEAR FROM US MORE ABOUT. WE HAVE A LOT OF FUN. WE GET TO KNOW THE MANAGEMENT TEAMS BETTER. ON THE BUS IN BETWEEN, WE TAKE SOME OF THESE BRANCHES, TELLERS AND BRANCH MANAGERS, AND ASK THEM TO GIVE THEM BEER AND IMMUNITY AND SAY, TELL US WHAT WE NEED TO KNOW SO WE CAN RUN A We take, you know, between some of these branches and stuff, we take tellers and branch managers and ask them to give them beard immunity and say, tell us what we need to know so we can run a better company for our clients. And you've got a very warm welcome here, which I'm not sure how many chairmen so far up the chain would get. Is that something that warms you, that you take a lot of positivity from? Yeah. I mean, look, I love our people. And, you know, this is our 10th. This is the 10th anniversary of Wambauu which is why we're doing this particular state and then we're heading up to Seattle and yeah you look you know basically a company uses people. They deliver to your employees. They want to do a good job. They want happy customers and we talk about client obsession. We mean it but that has to start with me too. I have to talk to clients. I have to have them my lunches and dinners and town halls and and we have have to listen to our people because our people are the ones dealing with the customers every day. You mentioned the Wamuu acquisition. Ten years since that, you wouldn't have the footprint you have here in California if not for it. But you've also been a bit critical of some of those acquisitions you did during the crisis. Ten years ago, if you had the time again, would you do this acquisition again? Absolutely. Wamuu put us into California where we really were in Florida. We had a very small presence. Washington state. And we've gone from like fourteen hundred brands to eighteen hundred. We've gone from they didn't have small business planning here at all or very small. We now have seven billion dollars loans up from something less than a billion. So it's just a great it's been a great thing for those states in every community that where Wamuu was. We now have commercial banking, investment banking, private banking, corporate social responsibility and philanthropy, so it's been great. The negative I always talked about was we were punished, a little bit, after the fact, by the government on some of the bad things that Whamu did. But you know what, that's in the past but we're moving forward. You're one of the few big banks that's still actually expanding your branch footprint. That's more in new geographies than just arbitrarily having more branches? What's allowing you to do that? Is it the regulatory environment that it now allows you to push into that, or is it because you see weakness in some of your rivals in those geographies? It's the regulatory environment that had made it clear that it didn't want to expand. I don't know why. I mean, it's a wonderful thing to do. We are opening, we even announced, 400 branches pretty much between Washington, Philly, Boston, a few others. When we go to those towns, we do small business lending, LMI , lower middle-income housing lending. We do, you know, we do a lot of corporate responsibilities, so it's really good for the towns. I remember we already do business in a lot of those towns in credit card, private banking, middle market, large corporate investment banking. It does not add any incremental risk at all for those open branches. So we eventually want to, you know, go across the country and fill out some of the cities were not in. Let's talk about the broader and it doesn't add any incremental risk to open branches, we have to see if we're not in. Let's talk about the US economy. We had a 4% handle and the GDP. Do you congratulate the president on that number? Was he right to take a victory lap after it was announced. Presidents get a lot of credit and blame for things they didn't do but the president has done things which accelerated growth. So competitive taxes. We need a competitive tax. They've won, but in fact they have to play the risk and protect themselves. I believe America does not have the problem of going to blame for things we didn't get to, but the president did things that accelerated growth. Competitive taxes, we needed competitive taxes. The way the American public is thinking about it, for 20 years we've been increasingly uncompetitive driving capital and brains overseas. small businesses. They'll tell you about the crippling bureaucratic, paperwork, litigation that we've had less small business formation in America than in any other recovery. So, yeah, this has accelerated the growth. We had 20% over 10 years. It should have been 40%. The reason it wasn't 40% was because a lot of things that we did hurt ourselves. So, I'm hoping we continue to have policies that accelerate growth, and growth is good for all Americans, which is why it's so important to have some kind of growth agenda. It's 4% sustainable? 50% don't graduate. We don't give kids the skills they need. We don't let felons have jobs again. We have an opioid crisis. Like, take bureaucracy. It takes 12 years to get permits to build a bridge that's already there and failing. And it took eight years to put a man on the moon. So the American public looks at this stuff and says, that's what's holding us back. It was us. So it certainly should be a hell of a lot better than 2%. I don't know if the natural rate is 3.5 or 4 or 3, but it's not 2. Let's talk about the president's trade policies. We talk about the U.S. economy being strong, but China's GDP that just came out was 6.7%. If that trade battle with China continues to escalate, who wins it ultimately? Who can take it? Right now, I'd put it in the skirmish category. And the business community is pretty much represented to the president that we agree with a lot of the issues raised by china the business community in general would have approached it differently which is to get canada mexico japan and europe to have a common front to present to china the way trade should be done it needs to be fixed we want to be fixed he's taking an approach which you know i'm a little worried could create these negative outcomes we've told the president that i'm hoping his methods work if he comes more in It's a little bit of a surprise. If I go and tell him the question, he has to be fixed. He's taken an approach, I'm worried could create these negative outcomes. We've told the president that. I'm hoping his methods work. If it becomes more in the skirmish, if you do $200 billion more and you do the autotariff and all that, yes, I think it could offset some of the benefits we've had from the good things he's done. You said you told the president you disagree, what was his response? He obviously does agree with us. I'm the leader of NAD. AROUND THE UNITED STATES, NO I CAN'T TELL YOU I'M WRONG ON THAT. WHAT HAD TRUMP BEEN THROUGH? HE OBVIOUSLY DOES AGREE WITH US AND I HAD TO TELL THE PRESIDENT, HE TOLD THEM THERE WAS A VALUE, AND THEY WERE WRONG. HE SAID THERE WOULD BE NO EFFECT ON INFLATION. I think NAPTA should be done. They've been talking about this for now. It should be done by now. Mexico is a wonderful one of ours. Let's focus on China. You disagree with this tactics. If we considered the news that came out of his meeting with Jean Claude Juncker last week that there was progress between the U.S. and the EU, does that suggest that in the long term, you do believe China should get out of his meeting with John Claude Juncker last week, that there is progress between the U.S. and the E.U., does that suggest that in the long term, he may be proven right that this could all work out for the best? It may. I don't know any better than you. And do you criticize his advisors for giving him the wrong advice on tactics? No. I think they're saying there's been retaliation and if we do it, there'll be another predictable round of retaliation, and there'll be another predictable round of retaliation. And there'll be a mounting uncertainty and a reducing investment. And it'll eventually slow down the GDP, and, of course, no one wants that. We think there's just better ways to do it, but obviously, we want him to finish a trade deal with China that deals with the important subjects, reciprocal ownership, how intellectual property gets handled, non-tariff barriers and stuff like that. So those issues are real. They need to be resolved in terms of his team. Jamie, will you ever offered a job in his team? And given that you question the advice he's getting, do you wish you'd taken it if you were offered it? I'm not going to talk about conversations. I am. I'm very happy where I am. I love my company. I love my job. I know you do. And we will certainly be coming to that a bit more later. Just on the topic of the president as well, very quickly, the president said in a press conference just now with the Italian prime minister that it would be okay to have a government shutdown that related to the fact that he wants to get funding for his border wall. What was your response to that? I think it's been tried before and it hasn't had good outcomes. And it hurts a lot of people who really have nothing to do with the process. So I think the political process to learn not to use those kind of things get what they want. I understand the president's point but but this is that is not a way to be productive and conducive to growth. Let's talk about the Fed and interest rates. Jamie, if we may. The president made clear in an interview with CNBC a couple of weeks ago that he preferred lower rates talking about the Fed's hikes he said quote I'm not thrilled because we go up and every time you go up they want to raise rates again. I'm not happy about it but at the same time I'm letting them do what they feel best. Did he go too far with that statement commenting on Fed policy? Look a Fed is given their mandate by Congress and that mandate is quite clear you can argue was the right mandate or not I think the other thing that everyone should think in mind when this race is why are they not so if they're going up and they're going up gently if they're going up because the economy strong that net net is a very good thing so it's very hard to look at interest rates and separate that is one factor and you know it doesn't relate to the economy doing so I think as long as rates are going up and the economy is strong, we're going to be fine. When we look at the shape of the yield curve, a lot of people get concerned about the fact that it's flattening. Does that, to you, suggest that the Fed is going a little bit too fast, that they should take the foot off the hike pace for now? No, I think it's, again, a very simplistic way to look at it. That's one factor. There are a lot of other factors involved, and well, in history, that happened before. But we have growth. I personally think the 10-year bonds are going to be going up, not down and all in history that happened before but we have growth. I personally the ten year bonds can be going up not down again like I said for good reasons your natural rate to the ten year bond today with inflation two percent before percent. And so we've had a suppression of rates for the better part of the decade around the world. Those things reversing. But so far to good effect which is global growth is can be strong has been in a long period of time and America looks like it's accelerating. So as long as they're raising rates than that, it's fine. One of, when I think about your share price, Jaimie and for all of the big banks, it's been so tightly correlated with what the yield curve is doing. How do you think about that? Is that correlation overdone? Whether we get a slightly flat, a slightly steeper curve? Do you think people the share price reaction to it is overdone? We make a very clear disclosure what interest rates alone due to our P&L. Now, of course, that's not what the world is right. Interest rates go up now for a reason, but alone rates going up, short rates going up. Helps our P&L helps our profit line so but I think it's an overreaction to that. I think banks are all different. You know, we're going to do quite well as a bank regardless. We don't take bets and interest rates, but if you think that rates are going down the 10 year because the economy is weakening, WHAT THE ECONOMY LOOKS LIKE, YOU ASKING THEM, BUT THAT LOOKS TOO DIFFERENT, NO. WE ARE GOING TO DO QUITE WELL AS A BANK REGARDLESS WE DON'T TAKE BETS, BUT IF YOU THINK THE RATE GOING DOWN BECAUSE THE ECONOMY IS WEAKENING, IT CAN AFFECT BANKS. IN TERMS OF THE EQUITY MARKET THERE HAVE BEENOME OF THE SHORT-TERM PRESSURE IN THE LAST FEW WEEKS, FACEBOOK. THE NASDAQ IS DOWN SHARPLY AGAIN TODAY. WHEN YOU SEE THE MARKET REACTION . DOES THAT TO YOU IT SUGGESTS Obviously, companies that have very high PEs, when you forecast the future changes a little bit, it's going to dramatically change the stock price. But if you look at stocks, if you think we might have a good economy for a couple of years and their earnings are going to grow 5%, 10% or more, even if PEs come down because rates are going up, that's a very likely outcome. So I'm not saying it's going to happen. I look at the possibilities and probabilities, but the economy looks quite strong. Consumers are in good shape. Their balance is in good shape. There are no potholes out there. Lending has been pristine capital expenditures going up. More people are going back to work unemployment may hit post War low one point this year. Those are all positives and we don't have the leverage in the system we had in 0 7. There's only some kind of problem but that that is not the problem today.
